blocks.h: ITS BRANCHES IN THE SKY
Roya Publication No. 120
by Chew Z
For everyone who lost someone in that war.
And for the ones still waiting to be told who decided.
SYNOPSIS

Every school in that country is named for something. This one is called the Goodly Tree, after an old line about a good word — that it is like a good tree, its root firm in the earth and its branches up in the sky. The name is painted on the wall by the gate, in the good hand somebody was paid for. Nobody reads it. That is what a name on a wall is for.

A man who mends outboard motors can always find the part. Thirty years in one yard on Iran’s southern coast, nine thousand engines, and not once has a motor failed without something he could lift onto the bench and set in front of the owner. That is what a trade is. It is also, though he has never had occasion to say so, what he takes an answer to be.

His middle daughter is nine. She asks why the sea is a different colour out there, whether fish sleep, what the mud is for — and he can answer every one of them, which he takes to be the whole of what a father is for.

It is the last winter before the war. The money is doing what money does, so the yard has never been busier. There is shouting in other cities. His sister telephones from somewhere safer and is refused twice. His wife has a sentence that ends every conversation, and the schools are open.
Then there is a Saturday morning, and a man nine minutes away with a compressor running.

Afterwards the questions are his, and he asks them of an office. The office is not evasive. It answers him kindly and correctly on a telephone number that has never once rung out, by a woman who knows his voice, asks after his son, reads his case number back to him and tells him there is nothing further on the file at this time. She has told him that forty times.
He is not looking for somebody to blame. He has been in a trade his whole life and he knows what a cause looks like.
He is looking for the part.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

On the ninth of Esfand 1404 [28 February 2026], the first morning of the war, two cruise missiles struck an elementary school in Minab, in Hormozgan, on the southern coast of Iran. Girls were taught upstairs and boys downstairs.
The school was called Shajareh Tayyebeh, the goodly tree, after the verse in the sura of Abraham likening a good word to a good tree, its root firm and its branches in the sky.

Most of what follows is not disputed. The building had been the compound’s own headquarters. By 1395 [2016] it had been walled off, repainted and given playgrounds and three gates with no checkpoint, and the military had left about fifteen years before. The targeting data still described it as part of the compound, on imagery about seven years old.
In 1398 [2019] an analyst looked at that building, saw what it had become, and wrote it down. The note was filed outside the system that held the target code, and the code did not change.

More than a thousand targets were struck that day, through a system that had cut that work from hours to minutes. The company that built it has said it is not responsible for the underlying data nor for identifying intelligence deficiencies — true, and the most frightening sentence I read all year. The team at that command whose job was to think about civilians had gone from ten to one. No civilian-harm specialist looked at the site; none was required to.

The head teacher understood what was happening before anybody else in that building, ordered the school closed and had the parents telephoned. Many could not get there. Twenty minutes later the first missile struck; a second struck the room where the survivors had been gathered; that afternoon a third hit the clinic treating the injured.

I am not going to give you a number, and the refusal is the point. On the first afternoon it was five. The official count was a hundred and fifty-six. In Tir [July] the forensic department reported sixty-two fragments identified, by DNA, as thirty-two children.

Three were never found at all. Each figure was given in good faith by somebody who needed it to be that one, and a novel that picked between them would be telling you something nobody has earned the right to tell you.

What is invented is the family — Mansour, Halimeh, Golnar, Zeynab, Younes, the yard and the boat — and the journalist, the man from the province and the analyst. Nothing in their lives is borrowed from the real families, who are alive and were named in reporting I have not used. Everything else above is not invented.
The paperback he is handed is a real book: Robert M. Pirsig’s Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, 1974. Not a line of it is quoted here.

Nine months on: no report, no prosecution, no apology, no money. A United Nations mission has found reasonable grounds to believe a war crime was committed and that the school was the intended point of impact. The President of the United States has said, at various times, that Iran did it, that mistakes are made, and that nobody would ever be able to say what happened there.

Amnesty, which called the strike unlawful, also said the Iranian authorities should not have put a school against a military compound, and recorded that they staged mass funerals and filmed traumatised children. The people in this book stand between two machineries, not behind one.

What I could not stop thinking about is how quickly we became able to hear it. There is a day of it, and a week, and then it is a file somebody is waiting on. Nobody decides to stop feeling it; it costs something, the price rises, and at some point we stopped paying. I watched myself do it about Gaza, where the shape is the same: children killed, an investigation promised, a finding that never arrives, a fortnight of outrage, a weekend.
I have not named a single real person in the body of this book. The dead children of Minab have names, their families know them, and it is not my business to use them to make you cry.
Chew Z
I. THE QUESTIONS
WHY IS THE SEA THAT COLOUR OVER THERE AND NOT HERE?
Because of the sand.
The Qoroqi boy put a shear pin in backwards, which cannot be done, and did it anyway, and I walked down to the channel to see the damage before his father came to argue with me about the price.
Golnar came because she was five and because anything was better than the house.

End of Ordibehesht, the heat already standing up off the mud in sheets. She had her sandals in her hand. She always had her sandals in her hand; she carried them the way a man carries a tool he intends to use later.
Out past the mouth the water was the colour of the inside of a shell. Close in it was brown and slow and had a skin on it.
She said, why is it that colour over there and not here, and I said, because of the sand.
She looked at it a long time. Then she said: so if I walked out there, I would be clean.

The propeller was ruined. I told the father it was ruined and he told me it was not, and we stood in the sun for twenty minutes establishing that it was, which is a thing men here do instead of a greeting. You could hear us from the far bank. Two men shouting at each other in the flat light over a bent piece of bronze, and the water going slap, slap under the hulls the whole time, patient, like something waiting for us to finish.
She sat on the step through all of it with her chin on her knees, and when we walked back up she asked whether the sand went all the way to the other side.
I said I did not know.
She said, you should find out.
DO FISH SLEEP?
Yes. Not like us.

I never did find out whether the sand goes all the way to the other side. I have not found out since. It is the kind of thing a man means to look up and does not get round to, and then there is nobody left to tell.

She started coming to the yard after school at six, because Halimeh decided an hour of me was worth more than an hour of the television, and because the younger one had reached the age of touching everything and she wanted one of them out of the house.

Six o’clock in that yard in summer is the best hour of the day and the worst air. The sun has come off the tin by then but the tin has not finished with it, and you can stand a metre from that wall and feel it handing the day back to you. Two-stroke, hot metal, and the dirty-sweet thing that comes off a gearcase when you crack it. Halimeh will not come past the gate between Khordad and Mehr. She says the smell gets into her hair and she is right.

She was not useful. Men in this trade describe their daughters in these rooms as though a child of six can hold a torque wrench. She could not. What she could do was sit on the drum by the gate with her feet not reaching the ground, and narrate.

She did the street. Who had gone past, who had gone past twice, what Hajji Davoud from the ice place was carrying and whether it was suspicious. She had established that he was a very rich man on the evidence that he owned ice, and nothing I ever said about that made the smallest difference to her.

And she asked. She asked what a motor cost and I told her, and she was outraged, and she stayed outraged for a year and brought it up at unrelated moments like a woman in a long marriage. She asked why the sea was salty and I told her the rivers carry the salt down, and she said that was backwards and refused it.

One evening I had a gearcase open on the bench and she came and put her chin on the edge of it, which is the only part of that bench low enough for a child, and asked me what the little hole on the side was for. That is the telltale, I said, and if water comes out of it the motor is cooling, and if no water comes out you stop.
She loved that. For months after it she came through the gate and said, is it telling you.

It was the same evening, with the light going and the first of the moths already at the bulb, that she asked whether fish sleep. I said yes, not like us — that you cannot really tell, because they do not shut their eyes. They go still, and they go down, and they stop being interested in anything.

She considered this a while, with her chin still on the bench. Then she said: so they are asleep, but they are looking at you. I said something like that. She said she did not care for that and would like to change the subject, and we changed the subject, and discussed Hajji Davoud.
Then, at the door: then how do you know they are asleep and not just pretending.
I have been asked harder questions since and answered them faster.
from her exercise book
انشا
Subject: My Father’s Job

My father’s job is to fix the motors of boats. The motors are called outboard and they sit on the back and they are very heavy and he can lift one by himself but he says he should not and he does it anyway.

When a motor is broken the man brings it in a wheelbarrow or on the back of a Nissan and he puts it on the stand in our yard. Then my father looks at it for a long time without touching it. This is the most important part. My father says you must look before you touch or you will only find the thing you already thought it was.

Then he takes it apart. There are many small pieces and he puts them on a cloth in the order he took them out, so he can put them back in the opposite order. The cloth is green. If somebody moves the cloth it is a catastrophe.

There is a small hole on the side called the telltale. If water comes out of it the motor is happy. If no water comes out you must stop straight away or it will be destroyed. I think this is a good design because the motor is telling you.
My father has a scar on his left hand from a propeller. He was nineteen. He does not like to talk about it but if you ask him twice he will tell you.

My father is not a famous man and he has not been to any other country. But every boat that goes out of our channel has been in our yard and he has had his hands inside it. So in a way he has been everywhere they have been.
In conclusion, we should respect people who fix things, because if nobody fixed things then everything would only be new once and then be rubbish forever.
Marks: 18 out of 20. Good observation. Watch your handwriting.
WHO IS IN CHARGE OF US?
I said their mother. That was the correct answer and it was not the true one.
The blue cup is the one with the chip out of the rim and it was the only cup in that house worth having, for no reason anybody could have given you.

Younes wanted it. Zeynab had it, on the grounds that she had got there first, which was true and which is the only argument that child has ever needed. He had gone red and gone quiet, which is the stage before the noise, and she had turned her shoulder to him and was drinking out of it slowly to make a point.
I was in the doorway with a rag in my hands and oil to the wrist and I did not go in, because I had learned by then that going in makes it last longer.

Golnar came through from the yard with her sandals in her hand. She took the cup out of her sister’s hand without appearing to, gave it to Younes, said something to Zeynab I could not hear from where I was standing — and Zeynab laughed. Laughed, that child. The whole thing was over in nine seconds and all three of them were happy, and she went back out to the yard and never mentioned it.
She was eight.
I have run a business for nineteen years and I could not do that in a week.

There are three of them and they are a government. Zeynab is the law and does not enjoy it — at twelve she has the face of a woman doing sums in a shop, and she polices that whole household for fairness, which means she is the only one of the three with no fun in her, and she knows it, and it is the great grievance of her life. Younes is the weather. He is four and he arrives in a room the way rain arrives.
And Golnar ran the country.

And this is the part I would want a stranger to know about her: she was not good. She was kind about an hour a day and the rest of the time she was a nine-year-old, which is to say she was a tyrant about the television and vile to her brother in the particular way only a sister can be, in a low voice, with the door shut, so that nothing can be proved.

But she held them. The three of them had a country and she ran it, and when she was out of the house for an afternoon the other two did not know what to do with each other and sat in separate rooms like a parliament that has lost its chairman.
Halimeh says I have the order of them wrong. Halimeh says Zeynab held that house and Golnar only looked as though she did. We have never settled it.
WHY DOES THE OLD WOMAN AT THE MARKET HAVE A BIRD ON HER FACE?
It is called a boregheh. I said it was a kind of hat. She did not accept this.
You cannot explain the Thursday market to anybody who has not stood in it.

It starts under the trees before light and by nine it is a thing with its own weather. The Bandari women come down from the villages and sit on the ground behind what they have brought — dates in sacks, lemons, dried fish, tamarind, black salt, herbs tied with a strip of palm. And some of them wear the boregheh [bo-re-GHEH], the mask, a stiff panel of dyed cloth across the face with a ridge down the nose like the beak of a bird, gold-red or black depending where she is from and how old she is.
My mother wore one. By that year there were perhaps nine women in the whole market still in them, all past sixty.
She was seven and she stopped in front of a woman selling limes and looked at her the way children look, with the entire face and no manners in it at all.
I said, do not stare.
She said, why does she have a bird on her face. I said it was a kind of hat. She said it was not a hat, it was on the wrong part.

The woman had heard every word. She had been hearing children for fifty years. She put down the limes and leaned forward and said, in Bandari: come here and look properly. You are looking from too far away.

And of course she went. She went right up and put her hands on the woman’s knees and looked, and the woman turned her face slowly left and right so she could see it from the sides, the way you show a dress.
Then she said: now you have seen it, and you do not have to look any more. Now buy something.

I bought four kilos of limes I did not need. We carried them home between us, one handle each, and she asked the entire way whether the woman could eat in it, whether she slept in it, whether you are given it at a certain age like a licence.
I did not know one of the answers, and she said that for a grown man I knew a surprising amount of nothing.
That night she asked whether the woman could take it off. I said of course she can take it off, she is a person. She said then why doesn’t she.
Mansour will tell you about her talking, because she talked at him. She talked at him because he answered; she would have talked at the wall if the wall had answered.
With me she did not talk. She arrived.
She came into a room and the room had her in it, and I could be at the sink with my back turned and know which of the three had come in by the change in the air behind me.
What I have of her is her hands.

The callus on the second finger from holding a pencil in a fist, wrong, which I corrected for four years and never once changed. The nails, which she bit, and which I painted anyway on Thursdays because she liked the smell more than the colour. The way she held my wrist and not my hand when we crossed the road, which she started at three and never stopped, and which I have never understood, and which I did not ask about because some things you do not ask a child in case they stop.

And her feet, which were the ugliest feet of any child in this town — wide and flat and hard as a man’s from going barefoot on ground that would take the skin off you. In the evening I would put them in my lap and press the arches with my thumbs and tell her they were ruined, and she would lie back with her arms over her face and say good. Ruined. I am glad.
She is nine this year, and I have begun to see the edge of the time when she will not need me, and it is further off than I feared and closer than I would like.

That is the whole weather of being a mother, if anybody asks. It is not worry. It is standing on a beach in the evening watching the light go, and knowing that it goes every day, and that this is the correct and proper behaviour of light, and wanting all the same to put your hand out.

He thinks Golnar ran that house. She did not run that house. She was simply the loudest, and he has never been able to tell the difference, and I have let him have it, because it costs me nothing and it pleases him.
WHAT IS THE MUD FOR?
Everything. I said everything, and for once I was right.
Down where the channel widens there are the mangroves, and at low water the mud comes up grey-brown and shining and goes on further than a child can believe.
Younes would not go near it. He stood on the hard ground and made the noise he makes.
She went in to the knee in about four seconds.

It is the sound of my childhood and I have never seen it written down. Not a squelch. A kiss and then a complaint — the mud takes your foot and objects when you remove it, and if you go too fast it keeps the sandal, which is why she carried them.
Then she stopped dead and said, Baba. Baba. There is a fish walking.

And there was. There were forty of them. The mudskippers come out on the flat when the water goes and they sit up on their front fins like small angry men at a meeting, and when you come near they do not swim away, they run, in a series of flicks, and then stop and turn round and look at you.
She was eight and I watched the entire architecture of what she knew come down in about ninety seconds.
She said: you told me fish sleep in the water. That one is on the land and it is awake and it is looking at me.
I said I was not wrong, I was incomplete, which is a different thing.
She said it was not a different thing.

We stayed out there until the light went orange and the tide started to come back, and she tried for an hour to catch one with a lemonade bottle and did not come within a metre of any of them, and she told Halimeh that night that she had nearly caught one, which was a lie, and I let it stand.
On the way home she asked what the mud was for.

I said everything. The crabs are in it, and the small things the crabs eat are in it, and the roots are in it, and the roots hold the bank, and the fish come in on the tide because of what is in the roots, and the men who go out at four in the morning go out for those fish, and the motors those men break are what you are wearing those shoes because of.
She thought about that a long way. Then she said: so the mud pays for my shoes.
I said yes, in a manner of speaking.

She said she would like to tell the mud something, and turned round in the road and shouted thank you at the mangroves, very loudly, and a dog started up somewhere, and her brother burst into tears, and we walked home.

On the way back she asked whether the mud remembers the things that walk on it. I said no. I have since been told that it does — that you can read a tide in it, layer by layer, if you know how — and I did not know, and I told her no.
The first rain.

You have to live through the long part to understand it. From Khordad the heat comes down and sits on the roof and does not get up, and by the end of Shahrivar every person in this province is a slightly worse version of themselves. Tempers go. Men argue about nothing in the street. The children stop fighting because fighting is too much effort, which is how you know it has gone on too long.
And then one afternoon in Mehr the light changes.

It goes a colour I cannot name. Green is wrong, but it is nearer green than anything else. The dogs know first. The dogs always know first, and they stop and stand in the road facing the same direction like a congregation, and then the smell comes up off the ground before the water does — the dust smell, the one every person on earth knows and nobody can describe without using the word rain, which is cheating.
And then it comes.
She was nine years old and had seen nine of these and had never once been indoors for one.

I did not call them in. I want that recorded somewhere, because I have called them in for many things and I did not call them in for that. I stood in the doorway with a cloth over my shoulder and I watched the three of them go completely out of their minds in the yard.
Zeynab tried to be dignified for about four seconds.
Younes took his clothes off, which he was not supposed to do and which nobody stopped.
And Golnar did what she did every year, which was to stand with her face straight up and her arms out and her mouth open, catching it, as though nobody had told her where rain comes from.
They came in filthy. The mud goes orange here when it is wet and it gets into the seams and it does not come out of white, and I had three sets of school clothes in the tub until midnight.
I have thought since about why I did not call them in.

I think it was because I am from here and I know what the dry does to a person, and because there is a certain number of these a child gets. I did not have a number in mind. I just knew it was not infinite, and that one day she would come in from the rain on her own, because she would have got old enough to mind about her hair.
So I let her stand in it.
That is all. That is the whole of the memory and there is nothing else in it.
WHY DOES HE ALWAYS CRY WHEN I DO IT AND NOT WHEN SHE DOES IT?
Because you are better at it.

She was unkind to her brother in a particular way that I am going to set down exactly, because the women in this family have started saying she was an angel and she was not an angel, she was the second of three.
She never hit him. Hitting is for the simple-minded.
What she did was wait.

She would wait until he had got something — a cup of juice, a toy he had found, a small flat stone he was proud of — and she would wait until he was happy about it, and then she would say one sentence about it in a perfectly ordinary voice.
That one is the cracked one.
Those stones are everywhere, there’s about nine in the yard.
Baba gave me that cup when I was little.
And the thing would die in his hands. He would look at it and it would have changed. And she would already be looking somewhere else.
He was four. He could not even find the words for what had been done to him, which is exactly why she did it that way, because you cannot complain about a fact.

I caught her at it maybe a dozen times. Twice I lost my temper. Both times I was wrong, not because she did not deserve it but because losing your temper teaches a clever child only that you can be made to lose your temper.
What worked, in the end, was none of my doing.

One evening he got hold of a bottle cap — a gold one, from a soft drink, and it was a treasure, and he brought it to her to be admired because he had not learned yet, he never learned, he brought everything to her — and she looked at it, and she drew the breath to say the sentence.
And then she did not say it.

I was three metres away with a gearcase open and I saw the whole thing happen on her face. She drew the breath, she had the sentence ready, and then something in her went a different way, and she said: that is the best one. Where was it.
And he told her, at enormous length, for four minutes, and she listened to all of it.
She was eight and a half and nobody had said anything to her that day.

I have no explanation for it. I have thought about that evening more than I have thought about almost anything, because I did not do it. Halimeh did not do it. Nobody instructed her and nobody praised her for it, because to praise her would have been to admit we had all seen the other thing.
She simply arrived at it by herself, in a yard, over a bottle cap.
AM I CLEVER?
I said yes. It was not true and I would say it again.
I did not tell her mother about the bottle cap, and I did not tell her this one either. They are the two things out of that year and this is the worse of them.
Her teacher was careful with me about it, which is how I knew.

They are always careful. They come at it sideways, and they say the child is very sociable, and they say the child has a lovely nature, and you stand there in the corridor with your hands behind your back and you work out what is not being said.

She was not clever. Not slow — she was nowhere near slow, she could have done anything she wanted with her life and most people are not clever either. But she was not going to be the one whose name goes on the board, and by nine it was clear, and the woman wanted me to know so that I would not be disappointed later.
What surprised me was how little I cared.

I had expected to care. Men here care. There is an entire industry of caring about this, and half the arguments in this town at that hour of the evening are men caring about it very loudly at children who have been awake since six.
I stood in that corridor and the woman said, she is a joy to have in the class, and I thought: yes, and that is the thing, and you have just said it without knowing you said it.
Because she was a joy to have in a room. That is not the consolation prize they give you when the marks are poor.

Two men were in my yard that spring, ten minutes into an argument about a price. She came in with her sandals in her hand and sat on the drum, and inside a minute both of them were explaining it to her instead of to each other. They settled at the number I had said at the start. Neither of them knew she had done it.
She asked me that night whether she was clever, straight out, with her chin up, having carried it all the way up the road.
I said yes.
She said, Khanom said I was sociable. I said being sociable is harder. She said that is what people say when the answer is no.

I said: listen to me. There are two kinds of clever. There is the kind that gets the sums right, and there is the kind where you walk into a room and three people are angry and nine seconds later they are not. You have the second kind. I could not do it in a month.
She thought about it. Then she said, can you get money for the second kind, and I said not usually, and she said: then I would like some of the first kind as well please.
WHY IS THE MIDDLE OF THE ICE WHITE AND THE OUTSIDE CLEAR?
The air cannot get out. I was quite pleased with knowing that.
In the last weeks of Shahrivar we slept on the roof.

Everybody did. You go up at ten with the mats and the thin quilts and the water, and the whole town is up there, and you can hear four families having four conversations and a television somewhere and a motorcycle going along the main road at one in the morning with a load of ice.
The ice is the thing. In that heat the ice is the whole evening’s economy.

I would send her down to Hajji Davoud’s with the money folded into her hand and a sack, and she would come back with a block the size of her own chest, staggering, refusing all help, leaving a wet line up the road behind her that was dry before she reached the gate.
She was proud of that errand the way a man is proud of a trade.
One night she sat on the parapet with her legs hanging over and she held a piece of it up against the light and asked why the middle was white and the outside was clear.

I said because when water freezes it pushes the air out ahead of it, and by the time it reaches the middle there is nowhere for the air to go, so it stays there in little bubbles, and that is what you are looking at. Trapped air.
She looked at it for a long time.
She looked at it for a long time. Then she said: so the middle is the part that was last.
I said yes, and she said that was her favourite fact I had ever told her, and then, because she was nine, she ate it.

I would like to say what that roof was like, because people who have not done it think it is a hardship and it is the opposite of a hardship. It is the best sleep of the year. The heat comes out of the concrete under your back for the first hour and then it is gone and there is air moving, and above you there is more sky than a person can use, and the three of them would go down one after another, Younes first, then Zeynab, and then her, always last, always still talking, until at some point you realise the talking has stopped.
She fell asleep mid-sentence and woke up finishing it. I have told people that for years and I have never once been contradicted about it in this house.
Halimeh says she never once fell asleep mid-sentence. Halimeh says she lay there pretending, for the extra ten minutes, and that everybody in the house knew except me.
I taught her to make mahyawa and she was terrible at it and she did not care, and I have been trying for a year to work out why that afternoon has stayed with me instead of a hundred better ones.
It is a sauce. You have it with bread in the morning. It is anchovies and it is tamarind and it is mustard seed and fennel and black cumin.

It smells like the bottom of a boat, and then half a second later it smells like the best thing you have ever been hungry for. People from Tehran cannot be in the room with it. Every household on this coast makes it slightly differently and every one of them is certain the others are doing it wrong.
My mother taught me standing in the same place I was standing.
She wanted to help because her sister had been allowed to help at the same age, and the law in this house is the law.

She was hopeless. She had no patience for the grinding — you go at it until the seed stops crunching and starts to give under the stone, and she wanted it finished in a minute — and she had no hand for the amounts. You learn it by feel and she wanted a number, and when I could not give her a number she became exasperated with me — with me — and said, how am I meant to do it if you will not say.
I said, you will do it four hundred times and then you will know. She said, four hundred, and I said about four hundred.
She put the pestle down and looked at me with real horror and said: Maman, I will be dead.

And I laughed until I had to sit down on the step, and she did not know why, and that made it worse, and then she started laughing because I was laughing, and Younes came in to see what had happened and we could not explain it to him.
Four hundred mornings is a year and a bit. I had made it more times than I have done anything else and could have done it with my eyes shut, and some mornings did.
But she was nine, and four hundred of anything was the rest of her life.

We did not finish the batch. We ate the bread with cheese instead and left the mess on the counter, and I washed it all after they went to bed, and I remember being mildly irritated about that, and I remember it was the kind of irritation that is almost pleasure.
She asked me that evening how many times I had made it. I said about nine thousand. She said: so you have about nine thousand left.
I have done that arithmetic every week since and I cannot make it come out.
WHOSE WAS THE SCHOOL BEFORE IT WAS THE SCHOOL?
The navy’s. I told her the navy’s, and that we painted it.
She asked because of the floor.

In the room where the older ones have their lessons the floor is a different thing from the rest of the building — a hard grey composite, poured, with a drain in the corner of it, which is not a thing you put in a classroom.
She had noticed the drain. Of course she had noticed the drain.
So I told her.

When I was a young man that whole block behind the wall was the navy’s, the yard and the sheds and the long building, and the long building was the offices, and if you stood at the corner you could watch them raise the flag in the morning. Nobody from the neighbourhood went in. You did not go in. There was a post at each corner and a man in each post and you crossed the road without thinking about crossing the road.

And then — fifteen years ago now, maybe more — they went. Not all at once. Fewer vehicles, then the post on the east corner empty for a while and then empty for good, and then one year the flag was not going up and nobody could tell you when it had stopped.
And the building sat there.

For two years it sat there with the windows going and the pigeons in it, in a town where the primary school was running three shifts and the little ones were doing their lessons in a rented room above a shop.

And then it was given to us. I do not know by whom — a committee, a signature somewhere, the mayor at the time, who was good for this one thing and nothing else — and I remember the night it was announced in the mosque and the noise that went up.
We did the work ourselves.
That is the part I told her. The men of that neighbourhood did it in six weeks in the hot season. We put the wall across.
And we painted it.

I can still tell you the colour, because we argued about the colour for two days: cream to the waist and white above, which is what every school in this province is, and which somebody said was boring, and which won anyway.
Nine of us on ladders in Mordad. Tea at four o’clock on the step.
She asked me, when I had finished telling her all this, whether the drain was still connected to anything.
I said I had no idea.

She said she thought it probably was, and that it was a waste of a good drain, and that if it were up to her they would put the sink over it. I said that if it were up to her there would be a great many changes, and she said yes, there would.
It is the best thing that has happened to that neighbourhood in twenty years, that school. I say so to people who are tired of hearing me say it.
Nine minutes, and if I walk her down there, she goes in through the east gate, the one I made. I am putting that down while it is still only a gate.
It is still dark when the heating comes on, and the dog gets up because the heating is the dog’s alarm clock, and then everyone else has to.

The lunches are made the night before. This was a decision, taken in a kitchen, after a bad month, and it has held for two years, and it is the single best decision anyone in this house has made. Turkey for the older one. Peanut butter for the younger one, who has eaten peanut butter four hundred days running and shows no sign of stopping.
The bus comes at 7:14. Not 7:15. The driver is a man of absolute precision and he has been doing this road for nine years.
There is the thing with the coat, which happens every day.
There is the thing with the left shoe, which happens most days. There is a permission slip that needed signing and got signed in the car with the paper against the dashboard, badly.

At the corner the younger one turns around and comes back, because she has forgotten, and what she has forgotten is the hug. She does this about twice a week. She is seven and she still wants it and there will come a morning when she does not, and nobody in this family has thought about that, because why would they.
The bus takes them. The brake does the thing it does.
Then the walk back up the driveway, with the coffee, in the cold, past the recycling that should have gone out. Fourteen minutes before the first call.

The radio is on in the kitchen and has been on the whole time. It is talking about the thing it has been talking about for three weeks. Somebody is explaining what will happen if, and somebody else is explaining what will happen if not, and both of them are very calm.
Reaching past it for the milk, nobody turns it up and nobody turns it off.
II. BEFORE NOWRUZ
WHY IS EVERYONE CROSS ABOUT THE MONEY?
Because there is less of it. I said there is less of it, which was not an answer.

A man who would have brought his motor to the yard in Mordad brings it in Shahrivar. The next one brings it two months late. And then one of them does not bring it at all, and you see him on the water running it rough, and you both pretend you have not seen each other.
That is what happens to a trade like mine. Nobody comes and takes anything. There is no day.
They do not stop fishing. They stop maintaining.

By Azar I had the yard half empty and the work I did have was the worst kind — not repairs, bodges. Keep it going until Nowruz. Keep it going till the end of the season. Mahmoud’s brother asked me to do something to a gearcase that I will not write down because my daughters may read this one day, and I did it, and it held, and that is the year I had.
And the prices. You would go to the shop and the number on the tin had been written over twice with a marker and the third number was underneath on a piece of tape.

The thing nobody from outside understands is that this is not new. We have had this before, in the nineties, and in the time after the agreement fell apart, and everybody my age has a story about carrying money in a bag. What was new was the speed. You could feel it moving under you in a single week, the way you feel a boat go off the plane.
She asked why everyone was cross about the money and I said because there is less of it, which is not an answer and she knew it was not.
She said: where did it go.
I said nowhere. It is the same money. It is just worth less.

And she stopped on the road — the long wall by the ice place, four in the afternoon, the tar gone soft at the edges where it meets the dust — and said, and I can hear this, I can hear exactly how she said it, she said: then who decided that.
I said nobody decides it. She said somebody must — somebody must write it down somewhere.
I told her she was too young to be this annoying. She was not. She was exactly old enough, and I was the one who did not have it.
WHY IS THE LONGEST NIGHT A GOOD THING?
Because after it the days get longer. She said that was a very weak reason and she is right.
Shab-e Yalda [shab-e yal-DAA], the thirtieth of Azar, the longest night of the year, and the rule in this house is that nobody goes to bed.
It is a rule that is broken by Younes at about half past ten and by everyone else by two, and it is a rule anyway.
The ajil [aa-JEEL] in the good dish, and the shells going into a second dish, and by midnight the second dish winning. Tea from nine until two.
And the Hafez.
You close your eyes and you open the book and you put your finger down and somebody reads it out and then everybody in the room argues about what it means in relation to your life.
She was nine and she got a poem about separation, and her aunt — who is a good woman and has no sense at all — said oh, and the room went slightly quiet for half a second.
And then Halimeh said: it means she will be separated from her homework.
And the room came back, the way a room does.

Younes fell asleep across three people. Zeynab stayed up past her sister, which was the great victory of her year and which she mentioned for a month. And at some point near two I came out to the yard for the air and she followed me out, still awake, absolutely determined, with a blanket round her like a small emperor.
We sat on the step. It was cold through the blanket and there was no moon at all, and the only sound in that whole town was a generator somewhere over towards the market.
She said, so what is good about the longest night.
I said because after this one every night is shorter and every day is longer, all the way to summer. She said that was a very weak reason to have a party.
I said it was the best reason there is. You have a party at the bottom. Any fool can have one at the top.
She thought about it for a while and then she said she would like the watermelon without the soft part, and I said there was none left, and she said she knew, she was just saying.
Her aunt says it was not Hafez at all. Her aunt says we did Hafez the year before, and that in that year we did not have the book in the house.
I have the poem. I know the poem. I could say it to you now.
WHY ARE THEY SHOUTING IN THE OTHER CITIES?
About the money. I said about the money, and that was true and was not the whole of it.

Dey came and the bazaar in Tehran shut, and we learned it the way we learn everything here, which is that Reza’s radio was going in the shop and four of us were standing in front of it not buying anything.

Not a protest at first — a strike, the shutters down, which in this country is a language everybody can read. Then it was other cities. Then it was students, and then it was not about the rial any more, or it was still about the rial and also about everything.

Rasht is nine hundred kilometres from here. We heard what happened in Rasht on the fourth day and my wife put her hand over her mouth and the two of us stood in that kitchen and could not speak, and the rice went on behind us doing what rice does, and an hour later I went back out to the yard, because there was a cowling to finish.
That is what everybody does. I have not met a man in this town who did otherwise.
There was a bin burning at the roundabout one evening and glass on the road in the morning, and it was over in forty minutes and nobody I know was in it.

Hajji Davoud said it would be finished by Bahman. Mahmoud said it was already finished and what we were seeing was the tail. My position, given freely to anyone who stood still, was that none of them knew anything, which was correct and which applied to me.
She asked why they were shouting in the other cities. I said about the money.
She said, the money that nobody decided. I said yes.
She said: are they going to be told off?
And I laughed. God forgive me, I laughed, and I said: somebody will be.
Nobody has been.
HOW DOES THE INTERNET GET TURNED OFF?
Somebody turns it off. She wanted to know where the switch was and I said I did not know, which was the truth.
It went on the eighteenth of Dey and it did not come back properly for months.

First the thing in your hand stopped being a thing that works and became a thing you check. That is a specific feeling and everyone in this country knows it: the little grey circle, and you watch it go round, and you put it face down, and you pick it up ninety seconds later.

Then Reza could not take cards, and there were six of us standing in that shop working out loud between us who had paper and who owed whom and who would settle it on Thursday, like a village, which is what we turned back into inside a week.
Then my cousin in Bandar Abbas was simply gone. Not in danger — gone. No way to ask.
Zeynab took it hardest because she was twelve going on forty and her entire social architecture lived in that device. Younes did not notice. And Golnar —
She was delighted.
I have to put that down because it is true and because it is hers. For about nine days she thought it was the best thing that had ever happened. Nobody could check her homework against anything.

And the evenings got longer. We ate later and then sat on after it, and the cards came out on the same cloth we had eaten off, and Halimeh taught her a game she had learned herself in a blackout in the war forty years before, and she became ferocious at it and beat her aunt and did not stop talking about it.

She asked me how the internet gets turned off, and would not take somebody turns it off and leave it there. She wanted the room. She had built it already — a room with a switch in it, and a man whose job it is — and what she wanted from me was whether he did it with his hand. I said I did not know. I said probably there is a room.
Then she asked whether he knew us. I said no, there are eighty million of us, and I said it the way you hand a child a big number to make a thing stop being frightening.
She turned the number over for a while. Then she said it was worse that way, because if he knew us he might not.
He has told you about the internet going off. I will tell you what it cost, which is a shorter account and does not have a room with a switch in it.
This is what I stopped buying, in the order I stopped buying it.
The good rice. That went first, in Aban, without discussion.

The other one cooks shorter and comes up sticky at the bottom of the pot and does not smell of anything at all when you lift the lid. I put it on that table for four months and nobody ever mentioned it, not once, which is a thing I think about.

Then the meat went from twice a week to once. Then the once became a Friday thing and the Friday thing got smaller, and I got good — genuinely good, better than I had ever been — at making a small amount of lamb seem like a decision rather than a limit.
Then the fruit stopped being a bowl on the side and started being a thing I handed out.

Then the fish, which is absurd. We are nine kilometres from the water and I stopped buying fish, because the price of fish follows the price of fuel and the price of fuel follows the thing nobody decided.
Her sister came in Bahman and sat in my kitchen and told me I should send the children to her, inland, until it was over.
I said over when.
She did not have an answer and she was embarrassed, and I was unkind to her about it, and have apologised since, and she says she does not remember, which is a kindness.
What I actually thought, sitting there, was: she wants to take my children.

Not she wants them safe. That is what she said and it is what she meant and I knew it at the time. What I thought, in the body, underneath, was that a woman was sitting in my kitchen proposing to take my three children to another province and leave me in this house, and everything in me stood up.
So I said the thing that ends the conversation. I said, the schools are open.
And she said, yes, and left it, because she is a good woman.

And it was true. The schools were open. Everything was open. That is the thing about the months before — everything is open, right up until it is not, and the whole country goes to work and makes the lunches and complains about the fuel, and the alternative is what, exactly? Sitting in a dark house waiting?
The schools were open.
I have had that sentence in my mouth for a year and I cannot get it out.
WHO IS WINNING THE TALKS?
Nobody. I said nobody is winning, they are talks. She asked what the point of them was then.
By Esfand the whole country was an expert.

The radio in the morning, the radio at noon, the radio in the ice place, the radio in every taxi, and every man in this town with a position he would defend to the death and had acquired forty minutes earlier.

Hajji Davoud’s ice place is the coldest room in this town and in Esfand nobody needs it, and we went in anyway — four or five of us, standing between the blocks with the sawdust going dark under our shoes and our breath showing — and settled the future of the country in there, because it was the only room in Minab where a man could hear himself think.
Hajji Davoud said there would be no war because of the oil.
Mahmoud said there would be no war because the Americans were tired.

A man I do not like, who brings me a Yamaha twice a year and argues about the bill, said there would be a war and that it would last four days and that we would win, and I asked him what winning looked like and he could not tell me, and I enjoyed that more than I should have.

My own position was that there would be no war because there had not been one. That is not analysis. That is just what the inside of a person sounds like after fifty-one years of waking up in the same country and nothing having happened yet.
And underneath all of it, the actual thing, which nobody said in those words:
They would not. Not here. Not with the school at the end of the road.

Not because anybody had promised us. Just because it is the thing you have to believe in order to put a child’s shoes on in the morning, and every one of us was putting a child’s shoes on in the morning.

She asked me who was winning the talks, and I said nobody, they are talks. She asked what the point of them was then, and I said the point is that while men are talking they are not doing the other thing.
She thought about it. Then: and when they stop talking?
I said they will not stop. I had a shear pin in my hand when I said it. I put it in my shirt pocket and I found it again in Tir.
WHY DO YOU SAY IT IF YOU DO NOT MEAN IT?
I said I did mean it. This was not strictly the case.
I was not a religious man and I was not an irreligious man, which is the condition of most men I know and which nobody has a word for.
What I had was furniture.

I said inshallah forty times a day and meant probably not. I said alhamdulillah when a motor turned over. I did not pray with any regularity and I did not announce that, and if somebody had asked me in the street whether I believed in God I would have looked at them as though they had asked whether I believed in Tuesday.
In Ramazan I fasted badly and with complaint and would not have missed it.

And once a year, in Khordad, I went up to my father’s grave. Third row, and by ten in the morning that stone is too hot to put your hand flat on, so you sit down on your heels beside it in whatever shade there is and pour a little water over the writing to bring the letters up.
And then I told him about the business for an hour, and did not for one second believe he could hear me, and went every single year.

That is what I had. What happened to it later has made everybody want to tidy up what it was before, and it was not a faith you could put in a sentence. It was a floor. You do not think about a floor.
She caught me out on it when she was eight.
I had said inshallah about something — the gearbox would be ready Thursday, inshallah — and she had been watching me and she said: why do you say it if you do not mean it.
I said I did mean it. She said you did not, because you said it in the voice.
She had noticed there was a voice.
I said that when people say it they mean I will do everything I can and the rest is not up to me. She said that was a very long thing to mean with one word, and I said that is what words are for.
She said: so if the gearbox is not ready on Thursday, is that God?
And I said, without thinking about it at all, because I had a bearing race in one hand and the compressor was running and I wanted her to go inside: yes. If it is not ready on Thursday that is God.
The gearbox was ready on Thursday.
Zeynab came to me in Bahman with a face she had been carrying up the road.

She is the serious one. She was born serious and it has not been easy for her, and the great injustice of her life is that she does everything correctly and her sister does nothing correctly and the house runs on her sister.
She said: is it true that if there is a war they will close the schools.
I said I did not know.
She said that if they close the schools she will lose the year, that she has worked the whole year, and that her sister will not lose anything because her sister has not done anything to lose.
I said the thing a mother says. Nobody is losing anything. It will not come to that.
She said: you do not know that. I said no, I do not know that.
And she looked at me — twelve years old, in the doorway, with her bag still on one shoulder — and said: then why did you say it?
I did not have an answer and I have not found one since.

What I did was the other thing, the one that is not an answer. I asked her whether she would like me to do her hair the way she liked it, which takes forty minutes and which I had not had forty minutes for since Mehr.

She said yes. We did it at the kitchen table with the radio off, a bowl of water at my elbow and her head warm under my hands, and she talked about a girl at her school who has been unkind to another girl, for the whole forty minutes, in enormous detail, with a strong position.
And when her sister came in and asked what we were doing, Zeynab said nothing, and did not move her head, and did not invite her to sit down.
I let that happen. I could have said come and sit, there is room. I did not say it, because Zeynab had so little that was hers.
I have gone over that afternoon more than almost any other, and I still think I was right, and I still cannot bear it.
You begin for Nowruz in Esfand. Everybody knows this and nobody from outside understands the scale of it.

The house comes apart. Every carpet out, every curtain down, the high shelf nobody has looked at since last Esfand, the thing behind the cupboard, the window frames with a cloth and vinegar. You do it in a certain order and the order is your mother’s order and you are not free to change it.
For three weeks that house smells of vinegar and wet wool and there is nowhere in it to sit down.
And the children help, which means the work takes twice as long and is the point.
She was given the plate shelf because she was careful with the plates, which she was, and which surprised everybody.
Zeynab did the windows because she does them properly.
Younes was given a cloth and a chair leg and told it was the most important job in the house, and he did that chair leg for forty minutes.

And we grew the sabzeh in the dish on the sill. Lentils. She checked it twice a day and reported to me on its progress in the manner of a man giving evidence, and on the ninth day she said it was not coming on fast enough and should we buy one, and I said we do not buy one, that is cheating, and she said who would know.
I said I would know. She considered that and found it wanting: she said that is not the same as somebody knowing.
I told her to go and do the plate shelf, which is what you say when a nine-year-old has put her hand on something and you would rather she took it off.
That is the thing I keep. Not the big days — the three weeks of taking the house apart for them, with the radio on and everybody in everybody’s way.
Her sabzeh came on. It came on perfectly well, in the end, in the last week, the way it always does.
It is still on that sill.
WHAT IS THE FARTHEST YOU HAVE EVER BEEN?
Bandar Abbas. She did not believe me and went and asked Halimeh, who confirmed it, and she came back and looked at me differently for a week.
Two weeks before, with the house in pieces for Nowruz and her lentils coming on in the dish on the sill, I took her out on the water.

Not for anything. Hassan owed me for a coil and had no money and offered the boat for an afternoon instead, which is how half the debts in this town are settled, and I took it, and I took her, and I did not take the other two, and I have never told them that.
It was flat. That coast in late Esfand can be glass.

We went out past the mouth, further than I usually go, to where the brown goes and the other colour starts — the thing she had asked me about when she was five and had never stopped being slightly suspicious of.
I cut the motor.

You have not heard quiet until you have heard that. The water does a thing against the hull, and there is a bird somewhere, and that is all there is, and the town is a line behind you with the heat shaking over it.
She put her hand in and held it there a long time, the way she held everything, at her own speed, and then she said: it is the same.
I said what is.
She said the water here is the same as the water at home. It is not cleaner. It just looks cleaner from there. So you were wrong about the sand as well.
I said I was not wrong about the sand, the sand is real, the sand is why it looks like that. I was only wrong about what it would be when you got here.
She thought about that with her hand still in the sea. Then she asked what was the farthest I had ever been, and I said Bandar Abbas, and she said that was not very far, and I said no, it was not.
And she said: I am going to go further than that.
And I said, out loud, in the boat, with the motor off: yes. You are.
The last ordinary week of my life, and I have been through it so many times that I have worn it out, the way a photograph goes soft at the corners from being handled.
Here is what is left.
On the Sunday I cut her nails, and she complained about the left hand and not the right hand, which made no sense, and I did not ask.

On the Monday Younes had a temperature and was in with us and kicked all night, and she came in at six and found him there and was outraged and got in as well, and the four of us lay in the dark being too hot and nobody got up.

On the Tuesday she was horrible to her brother about a drawing and I made her apologise and she did it badly, on purpose, in a voice, and I made her do it again and she did it properly, and he had already forgotten and she was annoyed about that too.
On the Wednesday there is nothing. I have looked and looked. There is no Wednesday.

On the Thursday, the market. The limes. And a bracelet on the plastic stall with a bird on it, costing nothing, which I refused — I refuse that stall as a principle — and she argued, and I held, and we walked home with the limes between us.
She wore it on the Friday.
Her aunt had bought it on the way past on the Thursday evening and put it in her hand at the gate, as she had been doing behind my back for nine years, and as I had always pretended not to notice.
I have thanked her for it since. She does not understand why I keep thanking her and I have not explained it, and I am not going to.
Saturday, and the two fields are at opposite ends of the same complex, and the games overlap by forty minutes.
The chairs come out of the trunk. One of them has a cup holder that does not hold a cup.
There is a man who brings a thermos and offers it along the line every week, and every week about half the line takes some, and it is coffee, and it is not very good, and taking some is the point.
The older one plays defence and does not like it. The younger one plays whatever she is told and likes all of it.
A boy goes down holding his wrist and everything stops and both coaches walk out, and he is up in ninety seconds, and the clapping is the kind of clapping that is relieved rather than impressed.
At half time there are orange segments in a plastic tub and a bag for the peel and somebody has brought the wrong bag.

Afterwards, the oil change, because the sticker in the windshield says four hundred miles ago. In the waiting room there is a television on the wall with the sound off and the captions on, and a map, and the captions are two sentences behind the man speaking. A woman in the corner is on the phone about a different thing entirely. Nobody asks for the sound.

Then the mall, for a birthday gift for a party on Sunday, and the decision is one gift from both girls, which is easier and fairer and costs the same, and which both of them accept without argument for the first time ever.
In the car on the way home the younger one falls asleep sitting up with her cleats still on, and the older one points this out, and is told to leave her.
I can hold my breath for twelve.
Twelve is not very good.
It is good for me. My cousin can do thirty but his face goes a colour and I think he is cheating by going red.
My dog is called Pashmak and he is not allowed in the house but he is in the house, and my father says Pashmak is a disaster and that I am a disaster.
Everybody’s father says that. I think there is a place they go where they learn it.
Whose is the brown one.
He is not mine. I thought he was yours.
There are always a lot of dogs. Dogs follow children, everybody knows that, it is not interesting.
He has been asleep in the same place since we got here.

The bread at our corner is better than the bread at your corner. Ours is in the morning only and then it is finished, and if you are late you have to go to the other one, and the other one is for people who are late.
My mother sends me at six. It is still cold at six and the bread comes through the paper and you have to keep changing hands.
Mine too. Mine says if I am not back before the call she will know.
Mine says that and she does not know. She has never once known.
Does anybody else’s father do the thing with the shoes. Lines them up at the door, all facing out, every night.
Mine does that.
Mine too!
Why do they do that.
I do not know.
It has been a long day.
It has been a very long day. I keep thinking it is nearly evening and then it is not.
That happens in summer.
It is not summer.
III. FOUR DAYS
WEDNESDAY · 6 ESFAND
WILL THEY CLOSE THE SCHOOLS?
I said no. I asked three people that day and all three of them said no and I believed the third one.
The thing you want to know about the week before is that it was a good week for business, and I have never been able to say that out loud to anybody.

Men who had not serviced a motor since Mehr came in with money. Not because they had money — because of what money was doing. If you are holding paper that is worth less on Thursday than it was on Tuesday, you do not hold it. You turn it into something. A coil. A new impeller. The gearcase you have been putting off.
So I had four motors on the stand and I was working until nine at night under the bulb with the moths coming at it, and I was in a very good mood, which is a thing I have had to sit with.

One of them could not pay at all and had known it before he came, and he put a book on the bench with the air of a man settling a debt, which is what it was. Half the debts in this town are settled like that.

It was a paperback, Persian, printed badly on the thin grey paper they used in those years, and the cover was gone, so there was no title on it and no name anywhere. He said his brother had read it twice. He said it was about a motorcycle.
I said I do not have a motorcycle.
He said that is not what it is about, and left.
I put it on the shelf in the yard with the manuals.
And underneath it, all day, the radio.
Not news exactly. The absence of news, which is worse — a man explaining what had not been said at a meeting, and then another man explaining what the first man’s explanation meant.
Hassan said it would not happen because of the oil. I said Hassan had been saying that since Dey and that at some point a man has to be right about something or stop talking.
He asked me what I thought.
I said I think they will not, and I said it in the voice, the one Golnar had caught me using three years before, and he heard it and did not say anything.

I asked at the school gate that afternoon whether they would close. The office is the second door and it has a fan on the filing cabinet that turns left and right and lifts the papers under the clip every time it comes round. The woman had three mothers ahead of me and a biro behind her ear and she did not look up from the register when she said no. She said it the way you say a thing you have said twenty times before lunch.
I asked Mahmoud, whose wife teaches at the other one, in the street, with his hand on my shoulder, and he said no.
And I asked Hajji Davoud, who knows nothing about anything, in the cold of his own ice house with his hands in his sleeves, and he said no, and that one was the one I took home.
That is the whole of it. I did not need three answers. I needed the third one.
Zeynab did not sleep on the Wednesday and came in at two.
She is twelve and has not come in at two since she was six, and she stood at the end of the bed in the dark with her arms folded, furious, because she had failed at something.
I said come on then. She said she was not a baby. I said I know — come on then.

She got in. She is all elbows now, a great angular piece of furniture, and her feet were freezing, and she lay there rigid for about ten minutes and then she said: if it happens, does it happen to us or to Tehran.
I said nothing happens to anybody.
She said that is not an answer. You and Baba both do that.
So I said: Tehran. If anything happens it happens to Tehran, because Tehran is where the things are. We are a town with a fruit market.

And she thought about that and I felt her come down out of it, the way you feel a child let go, and she said — and I have had this sentence in my mouth for a year — she said: that is a horrible thing to be glad about.
I said yes. It is. She said, but you are glad, and I said yes, because she was twelve and she had come in at two and I was not going to lie to her twice in one night.
She went to sleep after that. I did not.
THURSDAY · 7 ESFAND
WHY IS HE NOT OPENING?
I said he must be unwell. He was not unwell.
Thursday market, and the third stall on the left did not open.

That sounds like nothing. You have to understand what it is. That man has had that pitch for nineteen years and he opens in the dark and he is still there when they are sweeping. If he is not there the women ask about him before they ask about the price of anything.
He was not there and nobody knew why and the market talked about it for two hours and reached no conclusion.

You can smell where that man stands. Nineteen years of split fruit has gone into the ground under that pitch and in the heat it comes back up whether he is standing on it or not, and it came up all that morning over an empty trestle.
Golnar asked why he was not opening. I said he must be unwell.
I had already heard, by then, from Hassan’s brother, that he had taken his family to Jiroft on the Tuesday.

I did not say that to my daughter at the market and I did not say it to my wife that night, and I have gone over why, and the answer is not flattering. It is because saying it out loud would have required me to have an opinion about it, and my opinion would have had to be either he is a fool or he is right, and I did not want to hold either one of those in my mouth at a fruit stall.
So I said he must be unwell, and bought the limes, and we walked home.

She wore the bracelet. She had worn it every day for nine days by then and the bird on it had already lost most of its paint, because it cost nothing, because it was from the stall I refuse on principle.

She had the bracelet on at supper. There was no paint left on the bird at all and she did not care. My sister had bought it nine days before at the stall I had refused it at, and fastened it on her wrist at the gate, and I had done about that what I always did, which was to see nothing.

My sister telephoned on the Thursday evening and I took it standing up at the counter with my hands wet, because that is when the telephone goes, and we had the conversation again and it went worse than the first one.
She said: send me Younes at least.
Not all three. She had worked out that all three was too much to ask and she had come back with one, the youngest, the one who would not know he had been sent anywhere.
And I want to put down what I did, because I did something cruel.
I said: and which of the other two do I explain that to?

That is a question with no answer in it. It is not a question. It is a door being shut and dressed up as a difficulty, and she is my sister and she heard exactly what it was, and she went quiet, and then she said all right, and asked about Zeynab’s eyes, which have been a thing this year.
We talked about Zeynab’s eyes for ten minutes.
Then at the end she said — carefully, the way you put something down on a table rather than hand it to someone — she said: Halimeh, there is nothing shameful in going.
And I said: nobody is going anywhere, the schools are open.

That sentence. Again. I have used it perhaps forty times that month and I have never once examined it, and it is the most frightening thing I have ever discovered about myself: that I had a sentence that ended conversations, and I used it, and I never asked myself whether it was true. It was true. The schools were open. It was true and it was the shape of a reason and it was not a reason.
FRIDAY · 8 ESFAND
CAN WE DO IT AGAIN TOMORROW?
I said tomorrow is a school day. She said the day after, then. I said we will see.
Friday. Nobody works. And because the week had been good I did the thing I had been promising since Mehr, which is that I took all three of them out in Hassan’s boat.
Not far. Not past the mouth. Just along the inside, with the motor doing nothing much, so that Younes could put his hand over the side and scream.

Halimeh would not come. She does not like boats and has never liked boats and the business of her not liking boats is forty years old and has its own jokes attached to it, and she stood on the hard with the bag and the water and waved us off with an expression of enormous suffering that was entirely performed.
Zeynab was in charge of Younes and took it extremely seriously and did not enjoy one minute of it and would not have swapped.
And Golnar sat up at the front with her feet hanging.
I will tell you the thing I did not understand at the time.

She had been out with me two weeks before, just the two of us, out past the mouth where the colour changes, and she had not told the others. Not once, in two weeks. She had the one thing in that family that was hers alone and she had not spent it, and she sat up at the front of that boat on the Friday with her sister and her brother and she looked back at me once and she did not say anything, and I understand now that she was keeping it.
I thought she was just looking at me.
We came in at four. Halimeh had the fish ready, which she had bought on the Thursday because the week had been good.

The five of us ate on the roof because the heat had come early, and Younes fell asleep on the mat with a piece of bread still in his hand, and Zeynab did the thing where she reads out loud to nobody, and Golnar asked whether we could do it again tomorrow.
I said tomorrow is a school day.
She said the day after, then.
I said we will see, which is what my father said to me and what his father said to him and what every man on this coast says when he intends to say yes and does not want to commit to the weather.
The last night I will describe is not a night I remember well, and that is what I want to put down, because everybody assumes I must have it hour by hour and I do not.
Mansour was asleep. I did the bags — I do the bags on a Friday for the whole week, so it was five lunches, and the lunches are the same five lunches they have always been.
I washed Golnar’s hair because it was Friday and because she had been in the sea.

She sat on the step with the bowl and the jug and complained about the temperature twice, once for being too hot and once, four seconds later, for being too cold, which is a joke in this house and which she was doing on purpose.
And then she went very quiet the way she did when somebody was working on her head, and she stayed quiet for a long time, and I combed it out and did the plaits.
Was there anything in that silence? No. There was a nine-year-old having her hair done.

She went to bed at ten. She came out at ten past for water. She came out at twenty past because Younes was in her space, and I moved Younes, and she said thank you in the tone of a woman who has been seriously inconvenienced.
And that is the last thing she said to me that I can be certain of, and it is thank you in a voice, about her brother, at twenty past ten at night.

People want it to be something else. There is a woman in this neighbourhood who has told me three times what her boy said to her on that last night, and it gets better every time, and I do not blame her for one second and I will never say a word about it.
SATURDAY · 9 ESFAND
ARE YOU WALKING ME?
I said not today.
The man with the Yamaha was coming at eight.

That is it. That is the whole reason. He had rung on the Thursday and said eight and he was a man who meant eight, and the Yamaha was the best job I had had in two months, and the gate is fourteen minutes there and fourteen back.
So when she came through with the bag I said, your mother is taking you, and she said, are you walking me, and I said not today. Monday.
She said all right.

She did not mind. I want to be accurate about this because it is the thing I have been asked about most and people want her to have minded. She did not mind in the least. She had her bracelet on and she was nine and Halimeh was taking her, and she said all right the way you say all right about something that is not interesting.
Then she came back for the thing she came back for, which was not a hug, it was her water bottle, which was still on the side.
She took it and went.
I was in the yard by ten past. The man with the Yamaha was late. He came at twenty to nine, and he was a talker, and we stood in that yard and discussed the price for a long time.
I took her at eight, because the man with the Yamaha was coming at eight.
I have done it so many times now that it comes out smooth, like something recited. It was not smooth at the time. It was an ordinary Saturday morning in a house with three children in it.
I made the bags the night before so there was nothing to do but hand them out.
Bread and cheese. A cucumber. An apple, which she would not eat and which went every day and came back every day, and which I put in anyway because you put the apple in.
I asked her if she had water. I asked her twice. She said yes both times and she was right both times.
Her hair was already done from the Friday so there was nothing to do to it. I said something about the plait on the left being looser and she said leave it.
Zeynab had already gone. Zeynab goes with the Ghaderi girls at ten to and does not want to be seen with any of us.
Younes was on the floor.
We walked down. It takes nine minutes and we did it in nine minutes.

Esfand mornings here are the only kind weather this province gets. The sun is on one side of that road and not on the other, and you walk on the warm side, because in a month you will not be able to. There were children ahead of us and children behind us, and a woman I have known all my life was doing her step with a short broom and said good morning to the child and not to me, which is the correct order.
She talked about a girl in her class who had been given a sticker for work she had copied off the board, and whether that was fair, and I do not remember my half of that conversation at all.
At the gate I did what I do.
I said eat your lunch.
I said come back soon.

And because it was Saturday and there was nothing in the day and nothing in the week and nothing anywhere in my head that said otherwise, I said the other thing, the one I have said every morning of my life as a mother and have never once heard myself say —
I said: like yesterday. Same time.
And she went in through the east gate, the one her father made, and I watched her as far as the step and then I turned round and went to the shop, because we needed oil.
The dishwasher starts its cycle at nine forty because it is on a timer and the timer was set in the summer and nobody has changed it.
The hall light stays on. It has stayed on since the older one was three and it has never been discussed since.

In the first room the younger one is sideways, diagonal, with one foot out, and the covers are on the floor, and they go back on. In the second room the older one is on her front with her arm over her eyes in the way she has slept since she could turn over.
The humidifier is in the closet. It came out of the room two winters ago and nothing replaced it.
Downstairs, the dog has got onto the sofa and is not moved.
The phone is face-down on the counter by the keys. It lights the counter up twice and goes dark twice.

The television has been off for an hour. Before it was off there was a map on it, and the map had been on it for three weeks, and tonight a man in a suit was saying that nothing had been decided and that everyone should be careful about speculating.

The coffee is set for the morning. The lunches are made. The one with the turkey is labelled in pen on the bag because last week they were given out the wrong way round and there was a whole thing about it.
Lights off at the bottom of the stairs, then the kitchen, then the porch.
Outside the sprinklers are not on, because it is February.
What are grown-ups actually for.
They are for money.
No, but properly. They get up and they go and they are tired and they come back and they are tired and they do it again. What is it for.
It is for us.
That is what my mother says. That cannot be right, because they were doing it before us.
Here is a thing I have noticed and nobody can explain it. When a grown-up does not know something, they get angry. When we do not know something, we ask. They have it backwards.
Mine says because I said so.
Mine says you will understand when you are older.
Mine says do not ask me that now. Not ever do not ask me that. Always now. There is a time when it would be all right and it is never this time.
The big girl talked to me. The big one, with the — you know. The big one.
Oh. Her. She talked to me as well.
What did she say to you?
I cannot say it the way she said it.
Neither can I.
I want to say something and nobody laugh.
Nobody will laugh.
Somebody made a mistake.
Yes.
No, listen. Somebody made a very big mistake. And here is the part I cannot work out. Nobody has been told off.
In my house, if you break the small jug you are told off before you have finished breaking it.
In my house too.
So why has nobody been told off.
Maybe they have and we did not hear.
We would have heard. You can hear a person being told off from the end of the street.
Maybe they have not found out yet.
Found out what.
That it was a mistake. Somebody has to go and tell them, and then they will be told off, and then it will be finished.
Who tells them.
I do not know. A big person. The biggest one.
Then that is all right. We can wait.
Yes. We can wait.
It is not even very long.
IV. THE WORK
I was at Reza’s buying oil.
Not cooking oil. The other kind, two-stroke, for Mansour, because he had said on the Thursday that he was down to a half-tin and I was going past.
There were four of us in there. Reza, and a woman I know by sight who buys for her son’s shop, and a boy of about sixteen, and me.
The radio was on because the radio was always on.

And then the radio stopped being a thing in the background and became a thing in the room, and Reza turned round and put his hand flat on the counter, which I remember, and the woman said where, and he said Tehran, and the boy said something about Bandar Abbas.
